title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
description: The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.In another world, Andy Burn
body: The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports. And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move. The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow".Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK?This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout. Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers.This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry.However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced.No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports.Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape.In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market.But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports.The government's own assessment is that the economy will gain £5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040.Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation. The classic example of the benefits of post-Brexit autonomy has been the development of precision-bred foodstuffs, such as Vitamin D-enhanced tomatoes. The producer of this technology has, however, backed the deal after the government negotiated an "exception period" for ongoing UK sale. Professor Cristobal Uauy of the John Innes Centre said that "aligning with the EU market will bring our science to a greater number of people".Bringing all the agreements on food, emissions and the youth experience together, the economy is forecast to get an overall boost of 0.5%, or £17bn a year.A modest boost, but high by the standards of past post-Brexit trade deals, for example, with Australia, India or Japan and the Gulf and the trans-pacific deal. This UK-EU pact actually matches all of those agreements combined for expected growth measured by the Treasury's own assessments.The biggest single boost to the overall economy would come from more European young workers. However, the economy benefit of this part of the deal per person reduces to zero, according to the government's own calculations.Burham also said he hoped a planned electricity deal with the EU would cut bills, but that has not been done yet, and requires a contribution into the bloc's budget for poorer regions.The electricity deal could help lower bills, but that contains a clear trade-off.There are still some details to be revealed in the full legal texts of these documents.The bigger point is whether this logic of gaining free-flowing access for food, in exchange for giving up regulatory freedom, will now apply elsewhere. Is food now a blueprint for future negotiations? It had been the Starmer-Rachel Reeves strategy to spread this model to other sectors such as cars, and chemicals. The big takeaway from today was that both the PM and his counterparts publicly acknowledged the end of the incremental piecemeal approach to aligning with the single market. The question is whether the PM thinks what goes for food applies across the whole economy. Most economists predict that could lead to much bigger economic gains, but it will also be a much bigger constitutional battle.

schema.headline: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow

title: Andy Burnham: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal
description: Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council Pres
body: Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council President Antonio Costa join hands at the end of a press conference during the EU-UK summit in BrusselsByRichard WheelerPolitical reporterAndy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year. European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.  Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week. Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.Figure caption, Watch: What the new UK-EU deal could mean for European relationsThe new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe. The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is "confident" a solution will be found, with Burnham adding: "Me too."On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data.Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel".The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028.Figure caption, Watch: Will the UK-EU summit deal boost the economy?'Brainstorming process'Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people. Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it."But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".'Endless betrayal'Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU."A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
description: Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged marke
body: Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO)  price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth."As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said."Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued.Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the company said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record.But tech stocks more broadly also fell.Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

schema.headline: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide

title: Grand Slam of Darts: Gerwyn Price survives match darts to reach semi-finals
description: Gerwyn Price faced two match darts before winning a thrilling quarter-final against Nico Springer at the Grand Slam of Darts, as Luke Littler's conque
body: Gerwyn Price faced two match darts before winning a thrilling quarter-final against Nico Springer at the Grand Slam of Darts, as Luke Littler's conqueror Jermaine Wattimena was knocked out.Three-time champion Price led for most of the match but his German opponent refused to let him out of reach.Springer missed a number of chances to level, including three darts at double top to make it 13-13 as he fell 14-12 behind, before he eventually made it 14-14 and then took a 15-14 lead.However, Price produced a stunning 143 checkout to take it to a decider in which Springer had the throw.The German left himself 73 after his 16th 180, only to miss double eight and double four for the match prior to Price taking out 78 with treble 18 and double 12."I'm quite lucky to come through that game," Price told Sky Sports. "I missed so many chances - I should've punished him."I kept him in the game, I kept missing doubles after doubles. Even though he was scoring as well as I was, I was missing opportunities after opportunities but I'm glad I had another one at the end."

schema.headline: Grand Slam of Darts: Gerwyn Price survives match darts to reach semi-finals

title: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
description: Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "init
body: Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.Denmark's security and intelligence agency said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attaché will now be expelled.Russia's Embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.In a statement posted on social media, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia". Russian state media cites the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly". Danish media named the target of the assassination attempt as the rapper known as Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Vasiliev.Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency.PET, which worked with police on the case, said three individuals were stopped while travelling by car near the music venue where Kyivstoner was set to perform on 25 September. Firearms and knives were found in the vehicle, PET said.Since then, two people linked to the case have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service.Both individuals pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported.In July, Russia's FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organising a "terrorist attack" on military facilities and personnel in Russia. The rapper denied this allegation on social media.In a statement on Friday, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the alleged assassination attempt was Russian "intimidation" and an attempt to make Denmark "waver" in its support for Ukraine.Russia's defence attaché must leave the country within seven days, Rasmussen said. He also said Denmark wants the EU to restrict the ability of Russians to travel throughout Europe, saying even though Denmark is already very reluctant to issue visas, Russians can still get a Schenegen visa in another country and travel to Denmark. Denmark wants these visas to apply only in the country that has issued them, he added.

schema.headline: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper

title: Dwain Hall found guilty of kidnapping and murdering Sonia Exelby
description: A man has been found guilty of the kidnap and murder of a woman who he groomed on a fetish website.Dwain Hall, 54, convinced 32-year-old Sonia Exelby
body: A man has been found guilty of the kidnap and murder of a woman who he groomed on a fetish website.Dwain Hall, 54, convinced 32-year-old Sonia Exelby from Southsea, Hampshire, to travel to the United States where he stabbed her to death.On Friday he was found guilty following a trial at a court in Ocala, Florida, of kidnap and first-degree murder. He was then sentenced to life in prison.Exelby's body was found buried in Marion County, Florida, on 17 October 2025 after she was reported missing from her home five days earlier.The trial of Hall, whose online username was Alpha Sadist, was told he had been the "executioner" of Sonia Exelby and had demanded she pay $4,000 (£3,000) for him to kill her.Warning: This article contains distressing detailsHall was impassive as the unanimous verdict of the Florida jury was read out.The court in Florida heard that the 32-year-old, who had struggled with mental illness, had wanted to die.Assistant state attorney Amy Berndt said on the first day of the trial on Tuesday that Sonia Exelby met the defendant on a now-defunct website and "he manipulated her for years"."He targeted her because of her mental illness and he exploited her for his own sadistic pleasure," she said."And when he finally got her alone, thousands of miles away from home, completely incapable of making any rational decisions, he stabbed her to death and buried her body."Berndt said Exelby had been "trying to find someone who would kill her," adding: "Unfortunately there was no shortage of depraved men willing to kill Sonia in the most torturous and vile ways possible."Sonia Exelby's sister, Gemma Isaj, who gave evidence during the trial, said following the guilty verdict: "A vulnerable person was preyed upon. A beautiful soul was taken."Our lives will never be the same again. We must learn a new way of being."When this tragedy began to unfold, Sonia really believed that she could stop others from getting hurt. And I believe that today's justice has done that."Furthermore, she shone the spotlight on the darkness of such sites, like Motherless.com. "In some capacity, we will continue to fight for mental health in her name."Her brother, Barry Wilton, said: "I know Sonia would be so distraught to see the aftermath of her death."Dwain, you pretended to care for Sonia. You didn't at all. You used her to fulfil your sick fantasies. "You had her life in your hands. You had the opportunity to save her, but instead you preyed on her vulnerabilities and you took her from us."

schema.headline: Dwain Hall found guilty of kidnapping and murdering Sonia Exelby

title: Andy Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more
description: Andy Burnham has hailed his deal with the EU as a "good day for Britain" and a "good day for Europe".In the hours before the prime minister spoke, it
body: Andy Burnham has hailed his deal with the EU as a "good day for Britain" and a "good day for Europe".In the hours before the prime minister spoke, it had become, if nothing else, a confusing day.That confusion was unleashed by an EU official who briefed reporters in the morning that implementing the new arrangements on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions would be contingent on the government agreeing within six months to cut university tuition fees for Europeans studying in Britain.That was later qualified by others in the EU - and straightforwardly disputed by the British government. And for all that it dominated the morning, it did not ultimately dominate or particularly overshadow what was a warm press conference between the prime minister and his EU counterparts, Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa.The settled position appears to be that negotiations on student fees will continue into the next six months but on a separate track, or a "different sheet of paper" as von der Leyen put it. This still carries some degree of political risk for Burnham, because if Britain agrees to reduce, let alone equalise, university fees that would be an economic hit for universities which would presumably end up being covered by the government. And it may still be possible, though probably unlikely, that a deterioration in those negotiations could pollute the progress of today's agreements.Conversely, expect Burnham and his ministers to talk up another area where negotiations will continue - on the UK not being affected by the EU's "Made in Europe" plans, an attempt by the bloc to protect its industries from Chinese competition.Today's achievements and hiccups alike may quickly pale into insignificance anyway. At the dramatic conclusion of his first party conference speech as Labour leader in September - a moment he has been dreaming of for decades - the prime minister vowed to get closer to the EU.Over the subsequent two months it has at times been a bit unclear how exactly he envisages that playing out and quite how far he is willing to go. But focusing on the process risks obscuring the most important development, which is that the prime minister and the government are now unambiguously committed to Britain not only getting closer, but getting much closer to the EU.There were two significant moments at today's summit in that regard.First, Burnham said that the government had got as far as it could go with incremental deals with the EU, at least this side of a general election. In other words, he has got as far as he believes is possible with the strategy he inherited from Sir Keir Starmer of getting closer to the EU within the confines of the post-Brexit architecture set out by Theresa May all those years ago, of Britain remaining outside the single market and the customs union. That suggests that after two years of this, there will not be a third annual summit to unveil specific agreements designed to smooth post-Brexit issues affecting specific sectors.Yet it does sound like there will be another summit next year - or, rather, an "informal brainstorming process" about potential options for future relations with the EU. That sounds pretty nebulous, sure, but an event dedicated specifically to both sides discussing how to change the terms of Britain's arrangements with the EU is likely to become quite a big moment when it arrives. Perhaps as importantly, von der Leyen made clear that the EU was embracing this event too. That said, it does diminish the chances of major movement from Burnham towards embracing a specific model for the EU relationship in the intervening period.And what of the domestic politics of this? Britain's seventh prime minister in just over 10 years watched from Manchester as the fraught relationship with Europe wrecked the careers of so many of those predecessors.Burnham's gamble is that this time it's different. He believes that public regret about how Brexit has played out opens the political space for a far-reaching renegotiation. Plenty of Labour MPs enthusiastically agree, and see this as the route to uniting the "progressive" vote at the next election too. Some, especially those who represent Labour's former industrial heartlands, are a little more apprehensive.This morning's confusion is a reminder that there is another element to this gamble. Negotiating with Brussels, even if both sides believe progress is a "win-win", can be a fraught and complicated business. Once he's on the other side of his brainstorm, can Burnham carry that off without getting bogged down and distracting from his government's other priorities?On the day he became Labour leader in July, Burnham described it as the biggest change moment in British politics in 40 years. He was talking principally about economic transformation. But going to Brussels and getting what he wants without serious complications would be a pretty big change too.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more

title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?
description: The UK and EU have agreed a youth experience scheme which will allow a limited number of 18 to 31-year-olds to work, study or travel in the European U
body: The UK and EU have agreed a youth experience scheme which will allow a limited number of 18 to 31-year-olds to work, study or travel in the European Union for up to three years.Every year, 100,000 Britons will be able to participate in the scheme, with a reciprocal arrangement for 100,000 EU citizens.A joint EU-UK statement says the scheme is due to launch no later than January 2030.The numbers for both those coming to and from the EU will be allocated among the member nations according to each country's population.UK participants will initially be able to apply to travel to one particular EU country but can later switch to a different one, staying in a total of three countries during their three-year stay. However, they must spend 12 months in one country before switching.Visas issued by the EU or the UK will initially be valid for two years, with an option to extend for one more year.Neither UK nor EU citizens will be able to access benefits while abroad or bring dependants such as children.Participants will need to pay an application fee and prove they have enough money to support themselves during their stay.There are currently no details on what application fees UK citizens will have to pay, but the EU currently charges €90 (£75) for short-term visas. Numbers vary between countries for longer-term stays. The UK charges £340 for its other youth mobility schemes, in addition to a £776 annual health surcharge. The UK government has not said how much money an EU or UK national needs to have access to in order to take part but for similar schemes the figure is £2,530. There are no details yet on how places on the scheme will be allocated if it is oversubscribed; however previous schemes have used either a first-come, first-served basis or a random ballot system.The UK already has youth mobility schemes in place with other countries, including 45,000 places for Australians, 8,500 for New Zealanders and 1,000 for Icelanders.In 2024, 24,400 out of a possible total of 81,100 youth mobility scheme visas were issued by the UK.Speaking at a joint press conference with EU leaders, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "These opportunities open horizons, and they create friendships that will last a lifetime."So it's a very emotional moment because these are the young people that will shape our future."One sticking point in the negotiations had been tuition fees and the EU's request that Europeans studying at UK universities should pay the same as British students.A typical undergraduate degree in the UK (excluding Scotland) costs up to £9,790 a year for a domestic student, while the cost for international students, including those from the EU, can vary from around £11,000 to £38,000.If the UK did agree to reduce fees for EU students, British higher education institutions could lose out financially. British students at European institutions pay non-EU rates, but these tend to be lower than in the UK, ranging from €1,000 to €20,000 per year.The UK and EU have not reached an agreement on the issue, but the joint statement says the two sides will continue working towards a deal and conclude negotiations by May 2027. The two sides have also agreed to continue discussions about the UK's participation in the Erasmus + programme.The initiative provides funding for students, teachers, youth workers and sports professionals to study or do work experience in the EU. The UK left the scheme in 2020 but last year the government re-joined for the 2027/28 academic year only, making a £570m contribution to the scheme. In the statement released on Friday, the EU and UK agreed to explore opportunities "beyond 2027". Some UK politicians had argued that the youth mobility scheme would disadvantage young people in the UK. Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said: "I don't think it's fair because it means that more young people are coming here to compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs."Speaking in the House of Commons on Thursday, Reform UK's Suella Braverman asked: "Why...are the government proposing to open the doors to hundreds of thousands of young Europeans who will come here and work in our shops and restaurants? "Is that not a total and utter betrayal of young people in this country?"Defending the government, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden has argued that countries in the EU with greater freedom of movement than the UK had lower youth unemployment rates.The Labour government has made tackling the large number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) a top priority.Alan Milburn, in his government-commissioned report into Neets, expressed concern about an "over-dependence" on foreign labour in the last 20 years.He said the recent fall in net migration had created "an opportunity for employers to reorientate back towards employing young people from their communities".

schema.headline: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
description: Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so."We're
body: Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so."We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in."We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia."Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear."I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November."You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said."We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.Meta has already broken ground on a data centre, external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres. Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".Google has been contacted for comment.

schema.headline: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas

title: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
description: Figure caption, Watch: CCTV shows explosion after Poland says airspace violated by Russian missileByPhoebe Hopson and Paul KirbyEurope digital editorP
body: Figure caption, Watch: CCTV shows explosion after Poland says airspace violated by Russian missileByPhoebe Hopson and Paul KirbyEurope digital editorPoland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022. Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents. Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support. Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine."It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy". In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable".Image source, Omar Marques/Getty ImagesImage caption, The UK defence secretary toured the site of the Koalicja operation with four other European colleaguesEuropean Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory. At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

schema.headline: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk

title: Michel Zecler: Police officers sentenced for beating of music producer
description: Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated
body: Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.All were told they could never serve in the police again.The case became a cause célèbre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.The case was heard by a panel of five judges.The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

schema.headline: Michel Zecler: Police officers sentenced for beating of music producer

title: Phoebe Bridgers: Fans use art to visualise phone-free concert era
description: Phoebe Bridgers banned phones at her gigs, so fans are using art to remember themImage source, Lillie CollinsImage caption, Phoebe Bridgers' concerts
body: Phoebe Bridgers banned phones at her gigs, so fans are using art to remember themImage source, Lillie CollinsImage caption, Phoebe Bridgers' concerts have inspired some fans to explore their artistic talentByNaomi ClarkeBBC NewsbeatPhoebe Bridgers has drawn in fans over the years with her raw, vulnerable lyrics and indie sound that can make even the messiest emotions feel less lonely. The US artist's third album Lost Weekend, released this summer after a six-year wait, delves into falling in and out of love, grappling with change and the confusing feelings that come with grief.On her tour of the Grammy-nominated record, Bridgers has introduced a no-phone policy - a move that's had an unexpected side effect.Instead of taking photos and videos of the shows, some are creating artwork as a reminder of the gigs.Massive Bridgers fan Olivia MacDonald, from Massachusetts, attended the singer's show in Boston last month.She was initially "shocked" by the no-phone rule, as employed by artists including Bob Dylan and Jack White, but became a convert.Without the distraction of phones, she says, fans chatted, danced and sang along with each other."Once I got to the concert, I realised this is such a unique way to connect and bring everybody together," she says. Image gallerySkip image galleryImage source, Olivia MacDonaldImage caption, Fans have used a range of mediums to recreate moments from The Lost TourSlide 1 of 4, Hand drawn sketches by Olivia MacDonald. One page depicts eyes with blue tears streaming down. The other page has a drawing of a guitar. The words 'You're standing too close I can see brushstrokes' is written around the sketches., Fans have used a range of mediums to recreate moments from The Lost TourMacDonald, a pen and ink artist, brought her sketchbook along to the show after spotting fellow fans' interpretations on social media. She relived the gig by drawing standout moments such as Bridgers' dripping, electric blue eye make-up and her guitar, originally owned by the late American musician Elliott Smith."Everybody takes away something different," says 28-year-old MacDonald."That's the beauty of it, that everybody can have a different interpretation."Sharing her designs on social media helped her connect with other fans, who reached out to discuss their experiences of the show. "I feel like with photos or videos, you capture a moment in time, and with drawings, you really capture a feeling and people can connect to that feeling," she says."It sparks more conversation too." Image source, Olivia MacDonaldImage caption, Fan Olivia MacDonald has been converted by the no-phone ruleBridgers has navigated an emotional whirlwind since she was propelled to stardom with the release of her emotionally charged and critically acclaimed album Punisher in 2020.The 32-year-old Californian has toured and won three Grammys with supergroup Boygenius, lived out a high-profile romance and breakup with Irish actor Paul Mescal, and lost her dad in 2023.Fans believe she explores some of these experiences in her latest album. MacDonald says Bridgers explained to the Boston crowd that the no-phone rule would allow her to talk openly with her audience like friends, without the worry of those moments ending up online.Some fans expressed worries the policy could exclude people with disabilities or those who might need to contact someone in an emergency.MacDonald says she shared the reservations, but points out fans were able to keep their phones on them and access the sealed pouches they were stored in at special designated areas inside the venue.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Phoebe Bridgers was propelled to stardom with the release of her emotionally charged album Punisher in 2020Fan Anna Meyer, who attended the New York show, agrees the device-free aspect made the show a better experience for artist and audience, and allowed the special lighting effects to be fully appreciated without being distorted by phone lights.The graphic designer, 35, chose to capture this element afterwards - focusing on a poignant moment when a kneeling Bridgers played piano in the glow of a spotlight. "It was so cathartic to feel so inspired," she says."And I do wonder, if I did have my phone, would I have felt this need to sit down and immediately draw something from the show?"Meyer feels the trend is particularly special as it's put a focus on techniques, such as pen and paper, in an age when traditional art feels under threat. "We're now in an era of AI where they want us to believe if you want to create something visual, you have to use a computer and AI programme," she says."And it's just not true. "We all have the ability to create, and our own creations that come from our own mind and hand are far better than anything that a computer can create."And sometimes even far better than anything that a camera can capture."Figure caption, Phoebe Bridgers fan Anna Meyer's time-lapse of her artwork inspired by the singer's gig had a positive response onlineFollowers of the new trend argue it also helps to guard against gig spoilers, where big moments go viral on social media before crowds get to see them in-person.Lillie Collins, a fan from Michigan, feels artwork offers "a little teaser" rather than giving everything away. The 20-year-old painted her own interpretation after seeing Bridgers' show in  Detroit and her videos revealing the piece blew up on TikTok.She says the wave of positive responses was "very exciting" as she'd never had that reaction before, and it's now made her consider that creating art could be a successful career route.Bridgers herself appears to approve too, as her team has shared several posts praising the artworks, external. MacDonald and Meyer were among those who got shout-outs on the official Lost Tour Instagram page, as was Collins, who says the idea Bridgers may have seen her artwork had her "screaming"."I really appreciate how she was able to bring this level of creativity and humanity into her performances," she says. Image source, Lillie CollinsImage caption, Lillie Collins got a shout-out on the official Lost Tour Instagram pageBridgers will kick off her UK run of shows at Manchester's Co-op Live on Thursday, followed by dates in Glasgow, Birmingham and London.Ayanoh Nakamoto was one of the fans who attended a special intimate show at Union Chapel, London, where Bridgers tested the no-phone policy.She will be back in the crowd for the first London show next month, and says the "excitement has built up so much because we haven't been able to see what is really happening in the US right now". "It's just so cool to have an experience where it feels like it isn't spoilt for you," she says.Despite Nakamoto running a TikTok page where she shares her concert video content, she admits it feels liberating to put her phone away and be in the moment. She jokes she doesn't have an "artistic bone" in her body, but thinks this might be her chance to try her hand at drawing, even if it is a stick-figure sketch."I wonder if this is going to be a stepping stone for artists to maybe have this at more concerts and just feel that connection back to the audience in the future."Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

schema.headline: Phoebe Bridgers: Fans use art to visualise phone-free concert era

title: Mamdani reveals plan for closure of New York's Rikers Island jail
description: New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of
body: New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.  Mamdani on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four new jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population. Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it by this year. But plans have been delayed over the years in part due to the logistical difficulties over where to place inmates. Dana Kaplan - who Mamdani appointed as the city's "Close Rikers Czar" told the BBC News channel on Friday that his latest proposal is not just about getting rid of a decrepit facility.  It is also a "generational opportunity" to "build a different type of detention system" and figure out how to detain people more appropriately, she said. The Rikers Island jail complex is perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, and has earned a variety of nicknames over the years because of its dilapidated conditions, including Gladiator School and Torture Island. The jail has housed a number of high-profile inmates awaiting trial, including Tupac Shakur, DMX and Harvey Weinstein. It houses more than 6,500 inmates at a given time. Mamdani hopes to reduce that number to 4,100 - a goal that has been met with skepticism by the New York City correction officers' union. "[B]uilding a new system that puts an arbitrary cap on the City's available jail beds is ill-conceived, irresponsible and jeopardizes the safety of all New Yorkers, including our Officers," NYC Correction Officers' Benevolent Association said in a statement. "The City cannot keep the jail population at around 4,100 without irresponsibly releasing individuals who committed violent felony charges." Kaplan disagreed."It's actually possible to have fewer people in jail in New York City - and that is what we should be planning for," she said. The jail complex has long faced backlash over staffing shortages, crumbling conditions and inmate deaths in the facility, including nine this year. Legislation required the jail to be shuttered by 2027, but Mamdani blamed lags under former Mayor Eric Adams' administration as well as the Covid pandemic for the delays. Last year, under Adams, a federal judge removed Rikers from the city's control, appointing an independent outside official to make decisions concerning the facility. In an 88-page report released on Friday, Mamdani said Rikers was a product of "deteriorating infrastructure" and that officials had a "moral imperative" to close it. New York City Council must approve the updated timeline, with members, including the city's speaker, indicating they support the plan. Mamdani's office said the city would open up four new jails - one in Brooklyn by 2029,  two in the Bronx and Queens by 2031 and one in Manhattan by 2032. The mayor's office argues the new, smaller facilities will provide inmates "access to daylight, fresh air and clean space" leading to better outcomes for detainees. The facilities will be easier for families to access as well, as travel to the remote Rikers can take hours. Mamdani said his administration would work to reduce the number of people being held in jail across New York City, including by offering alternative programmes to detention for some awaiting trial, by making it easier for families to post bail online and by trying to speed up the pretrial legal process. He also wants to open up hundreds of beds in therapeutic housing units for prisoners with serious mental health issues. Kaplan said Mamdani's administration had already opened 100 therapeutic beds at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan, moving 100 people off of Rikers Island.  The proposal involves a large investments: $146m (£111m) for mental health and substance use treatment and vocational and education programming inside and outside the jails.

schema.headline: Mamdani reveals plan for closure of New York's Rikers Island jail

title: Black Friday 2026: Can ChatGPT and other AI tools find you the best bargains?
description: Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of onlin
body: Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers currently go to AI tools for help.A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.Crucially, 36% of respondents who said they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't plan to use an AI tool at all. But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.OpenAI's ChatGPT came up with four options.Its top pick was a Hisense TV on Chinese retailer Joybuy's website, on sale for £499 down from £649.The next recommendation was a 55-inch TCL-branded TV, but a sidebar showed prices for the 50-inch version, from £379 to £814. Option three was the same Hisense TV as before, but for full price at £649 from John Lewis and Richer Sounds.This was the "best safer purchase" according to ChatGPT, as the sites offered longer guarantee periods. But clicking on the links did not go well. Both retailers said the TV was no longer listed online.The fourth option was equally fruitless - another TCL TV, at full price, £150 over our budget and not available online.At the bottom, ChatGPT served one last offer - "one OLED option to compare" - for a £1,100 LG TV that was marked as "Ad".While we were served up the same brands again and again, in reality there are tonnes of products listed for sale around Black Friday.Naureen Mohammed, who advises businesses on how to get their products to appear in AI results, told the BBC customers did not see the full picture when they talked to chatbots.If businesses fail to update their prices when people start hunting for bargains, "last year's prices are served up as today's deals"."I suspect the whole model for advertising is going to start influencing AI recommendations," she said.Her own analysis of chatbots' Black Friday tech deals in the UK suggested the big retailers came out on top - with Amazon mentioned in half of responses, and Currys following closely behind.Her tips include asking an assistant "is that this year's price?" and clicking on the links provided - "because you shouldn't take any advice from the AI system at face value".But consumer group Which? recently said inaccurate pricing in AI results added more work, external to Black Friday deal-hunting."If you ask ChatGPT for a list of 10 laptops under £400 and seven of the results are priced higher, you've likely wasted a good chunk of time going through them to discover the bot gave you only three options," said senior researcher Hannah Walsh."The opposite is also true - you could miss out on great models in your budget if ChatGPT tells you they are more expensive than they actually are."

schema.headline: Black Friday 2026: Can ChatGPT and other AI tools find you the best bargains?
